# Beware of Other License Plate Surveillance Companies Besides Flock


Flock deserves the heat it’s getting, but switching to another provider won’t necessarily improve anything


[Jay Stanley](https://www.aclu.org/bios/jay-stanley) ,
ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project


**Share This Page**


August 25, 2026


[Subscribe to the Free Future Newsletter](https://action.aclu.org/signup/free-future-newsletter)
[Or get immediate notifications of new posts via Substack](https://ourfreefuture.substack.com/subscribe)
*[Free Future home](http://www.aclu.org/freefuture)*


There’s a nationwide rebellion against license plate readers underway, and the company Flock is the focus. That’s natural, because the company has “[essentially dominated](https://ipvm.com/reports/flock-axon-home) license plate recognition across the United States,” as industry analyst IPVM put it. But Flock is far from the only vendor, and with Flock rightly receiving most of the heat, it’s important to realize that its competitors aren’t so great either, and that simply replacing Flock surveillance with another company’s surveillance won’t necessarily solve any of the privacy and other civil liberties problems posed by this mass surveillance technology.


We have covered Flock in depth, including in this 2022[white paper](https://www.aclu.org/wp-content/uploads/publications/flock_1.pdf) and in numerous[blog posts](https://www.aclu.org/news/tracking-alpr-cameras) since. A pioneer of centralizing ALPR data through the cloud, the company runs a vast “National Lookup” searchable nationwide database of license plate and other photographic data of vehicles — an inherently authoritarian infrastructure that has, among other things,[already been used](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/flock-roundup) to help ICE in its human rights-violating deportation drive, and to try to track and investigate a Texas woman who had an abortion.


Aside from being dominant in the domestic police ALPR market, Flock is also alienating many communities because of its[lack of truthfulness](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/flock-safety-credibility-lost-as-it-repeatedly-lies-to-city-councils-police-departments-and-public-across-the-country) and[erratic](https://gizmodo.com/flocks-ceo-is-sorry-for-calling-privacy-activists-terrorists-2000787247) and[immature](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/flock-ceo-goes-ballistic) public statements. Unlike its biggest competitors, which are public companies, Flock’s private investors include tech billionaire venture capital firms such as Andreessen Horowitz, which also funds other surveillance companies like[Anduril](https://a16z.com/announcement/anduril/) and[Skydio](https://a16z.com/investment-list/#:~:text=Skydio) , and[explicitly aims to invest in building](https://a16z.com/the-superhero-stack/) domestic law enforcement surveillance capabilities. These are legitimate reasons to avoid doing business with a company.


At the same time, communities can’t simply assume that their residents will be better off from a privacy and civil liberties perspective by dropping Flock and replacing it with another ALPR provider, as some customers have done. They should ask hard questions about whether they really want to create that kind of a system, and if they do, ensure it doesn’t function as a mass surveillance system.


### Motorola Solutions (aka Vigilant)


One of Flock’s most significant competitors is Motorola. This company, which has been expanding its police technology offerings through an aggressive acquisition strategy in recent years, offers a nationwide law enforcement data sharing system similar to Flock’s called the National Vehicle Location Service (NVLS), operated by Motorola unit Vigilant Solutions. In addition to collecting data from law enforcement clients’ cameras, it also runs a large separate commercial ALPR unit that makes deals for tow trucks and other fleet vehicles to carry cameras and collect data for Motorola as they drive around,[amassing](https://www.vice.com/en/article/i-tracked-someone-with-license-plate-readers-drn/) billions of plate reads (a claimed 500 million[monthly](https://drndata.com/) , subject to no apparent data retention policy). Known as the Digital Recognition Network (DRN), that unit sells its data for commercial purposes but also makes it[available](https://www.ra-comm.com/downloads/vigilant-solutions/PSL_Mobile_Hit_Hunter_MHH_VS.pdf) to its law enforcement customers for an extra charge. Motorola[tells](https://www.motorolasolutions.com/en_us/video-security-access-control/license-plate-recognition-camera-systems/vehiclemanager-lpr-analytics-software.html) agencies they can have “access to billions of detections beyond your own,”


Some communities may want to take into account the fact that this uniquely powerful commercial plate-scanning infrastructure is marketed to private companies, including auto financers and insurers, and not only for repossession but also for “risk assessment” purposes — even though[risk](https://drndata.com/analytics/)[scores](https://drndata.com/risk-scoring/) have been shown to[disproportionately harm](https://law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/05.31.22-McConlogue-Website-Version-1.pdf) low-income and other marginalized drivers.


(Note that following a 2011 corporate breakup of the classic American electronics company[Motorola Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola) ., the company Motorola Solutions being discussed here is separate from Motorola Mobility, a smartphone[company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_Mobility) owned by the Chinese company Lenovo.)


### Axon


Formerly known as Taser, Axon has built its business around that police pain-delivery device, as well as body cameras, where it dominates the market, and its cloud data storage service Evidence.com. Like Flock and Motorola, the company is seeking to become a broad “operating system of police departments,” which has ominous implications we detailed in a recent[white paper](https://www.aclu.org/documents/surveillance-profits-and-the-police) . Axon has been aggressively expanding its law enforcement products, including by pushing[premature](https://www.aclu.org/documents/aclu-on-police-departments-use-of-ai-to-draft-police-reports) uses of AI. Many Flock customers already have contracts with Axon for body cameras and other products, making a switch to Axon all the easier — especially since Axon is pursuing an explicit[strategy](https://ipvm.com/news/90daa9d8-f4cc-435c-b24e-4b9cc6170070) of bundling multiple technologies and services together in long-term contracts. That raises significant[concerns](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/04/beware-bundle-companies-are-banking-becoming-your-police-departments-favorite) over platform dependence and lock-in.


As part of these strategies, Axon is looking to build up its ALPR offerings — and the market for them, which (as the ACLU has seen firsthand) has included lobbying against state ALPR regulations and local surveillance tech transparency[laws](https://www.aclu.org/community-control-over-police-surveillance) . The company began selling ALPR services in 2021[through](https://www.axon.com/help/fleet-3/cameras-and-sensors/fleet/3/alpr/alpr-introduction.htm) its in-vehicle “Axon Fleet 3” dashcam and in-car camera product, and then in 2025[announced](https://www.axon.com/newsroom/press-releases/axon-announces-new-fixed-ALPR-camera-solutions-and-next-gen-AI-advancements-to-expand-real-time-public-safety-ecosystem) new fixed-camera ALPR products, including a “smart streetlight” that attaches to existing poles and power sources. Both products[feature](https://www.axon.com/help/fleet-3/cameras-and-sensors/fleet/3/alpr/faq-alpr.htm) AI vehicle recognition. Axon doesn’t impose any[data-retention](https://www.axon.com/help/fleet-3/cameras-and-sensors/fleet/3/alpr/faq-alpr.htm) limits on its customers and lets police departments decide how long they want their data to sit on Axon’s servers. It does have a default policy of 30 days, but that’s only a default.


All three companies offer products that blur the lines between ALPR and live video surveillance. “You no longer have to make tradeoffs when it comes to ALPR deployments — license plate recognition or livestreaming,” Axon[boasts](https://www.axon.com/resources/vehicle-intelligence-from-axon-is-here) .


It’s not clear whether Axon has any formal arrangements with ICE or other DHS agencies to access plate-read data collected by Axon devices, though the company does have a number of contracts with the federal government,[including](https://www.newspress.com/2026/03/11/ice-17800-tasers-220-million-price-tag/) an announced $220 million five-year deal to buy the company’s problematic Taser devices. That does not have the same privacy implications as sharing data on people’s locations with ICE, though supplying that agency and its often lawless and abusive officers with Tasers may violate the company’s responsibilities under internationally recognized[human rights standards](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/surveillance-human-rights) , and generally carries a moral stench.


Axon is[explicitly](https://ipvm.com/news/4602759f-eccd-443c-834d-324c4b4f37f3)[positioning](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l2YbQCviDzc&t=1422s) itself as a “more ethical” alternative to Flock. As the security industry analysts at IPVM put it in a headline, “Axon LPR Business Surges As Flock Is Embattled.” Axon has a particular rivalry with Flock over becoming a broad provider of police surveillance and data services — the “operating system of police departments” (with Motorola also in the running in a less high-profile way). I looked at that race and its implications in a June 2026[white paper](https://www.aclu.org/documents/surveillance-profits-and-the-police) .


### Other companies


There are a lot of other ALPR vendors. The DHS Science and Technology division, in a rudimentary Consumer Reports-style[roundup](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2025-06/25_0606_st_lprmsr.pdf) for police, lists 16 different providers. In February, IPVM[performed](https://ipvm.com/reports/lpr-rankings-2026) tests of ALPR accuracy and included nine products; another analyst[identifies](https://www.obscureiq.com/alpr-vendor-atlas/) 46 vendors in the ALPR space.


One provider, Rekor, provides ALPR services to the Westchester County, NY police, which is the[subject](https://www.nyclu.org/press-release/westchester-drivers-sue-county-police-department-over-mass-vehicle-surveillance-system) of a class action[lawsuit](https://www.nyclu.org/uploads/2026/06/NOT_ASSIGNED_YUKIKO_ANN_UMEMOTO_et_v_YUKIKO_ANN_UMEMOTO_et__COMPLAINT_2_7073552923092437301.pdf) by the New York Civil Liberties Union and other groups. Rekor offers rich vehicle AI searches as well as video clips of vehicle captures. It’s unclear whether the company has a current contract with ICE, but documents obtained by the Associated Press in 2025[revealed](https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/spotlights/2025/border-patrol-is-monitoring-us-drivers-and-detaining-those-with-suspicious-travel-patterns/) that CBP had had access to data from Flock, Motorola, and Rekor. Documents obtained bythe Guardian also[show](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/mar/11/ice-car-trackers-sanctuary-cities) that Rekor’s client, the Westchester County PD, has shared data with ICE; it’s not clear whether that Rekor facilitated or continues to facilitate that sharing. Rekor has a nationwide data[sharing](https://www.rekor.ai/post/rekor-systems-launches-public-safety-network)[program](https://www.rekor.ai/post/rekor-redefines-privacy-security-and-sharing-for-license-plate-data-for-commercial-and-government-users#:~:text=Rekor%20Public%20Safety%20Network) like Flock and Motorola, though it is much smaller at this time. Unlike Flock and Motorola, the company[allows](https://www.rekor.ai/software/scout#:~:text=Data%20processing%20location) for local software installation and data processing by clients.


The provider Leonardo (selling an ALPR product called ELSAG) also[allows](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2025-06/25_0606_st_lprmsr.pdf#page=42) for its system to be run on local hardware. ELSAG has attracted attention lately due to a very[problematic capability](https://www.404media.co/this-company-will-add-phone-airpod-and-smartwatch-trackers-to-license-plate-readers/) that it advertises: the tracking not only of license plates but also of devices through their Bluetooth and other wireless emissions. It reads unique IDs broadcast not only by phones but also by tablets, laptops, and any other wireless-capable objects that might happen to be in a car, as well as wireless components of the car itself, such as audio-video systems and the Tire Pressure Monitoring Systems that all cars are now required to have, which use Bluetooth. That’s an extremely powerful capability that in many cases will supercharge the tracking of individual people including passengers — and we should hope this “innovation” doesn’t spread to other vendors.


Most other ALPR vendors are small, and based on a non-systematic review of a sampling, often don’t offer some of the more troubling capabilities that their larger competitors do — though there are exceptions (such as the many advertising cutting-edge AI, for example).


The big network-effects advantage that Flock and Motorola have over their smaller competitors — the size of their customer/data sets — gets erased if communities decide to ban nationwide sharing. If you’re collecting and storing your data locally and generally keeping things simple, the smallest ALPR vendor out there may serve just as well as the bigger names. Companies like Flock, Axon, and Motorola are competing by offering to make law enforcement ever-more powerful and all-seeing; good civil liberties protections will have the effect of making ALPR devices and services much more commodified and interchangeable — something tech companies hate but which serves the public better.


### Civil liberties differences


There are differences among the leading US license plate reader companies on the dimensions important to privacy and other civil liberties.


- **Nationwide sharing.** Nationwide sharing of the kind that Flock provides significantly increases the scope and power of ALPR surveillance compared to purely local surveillance carried out by a particular police department. Preventing such sharing has been one of our[primary recommendations](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/how-to-fight-deployment-of-flock-and-other-mass-surveillance-license-plate-readers-in-your-community) for communities. Flock[says](https://www.wyden.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/wyden_letter_to_flock.pdf) 75% of its[claimed](https://www.flocksafety.com/products/license-plate-readers) 5,000 police customers[participate](https://ipvm.com/reports/national-lpr) in the company’s National Lookup network, making it an extremely powerful surveillance machine. Motorola seems to have fewer police clients than Flock but — in part due to its commercial DNR network — boasts of an enormous number of monthly plate reads that can be accessed as part of its NVLS sharing service. It’s hard to find data on their relative market shares, but these networks give their operators an enormous business advantage over smaller competitors among departments that want the nationwide search capability they offer. Axon has an ALPR data sharing[function](https://www.axon.com/help/fusus/software/fusus/alpr/alpr-search-interface.htm#:~:text=Include%20Shared%20Data) built into its search tool, but that appears to require an explicit department-by-department agreement to engage in such sharing.
- **Retention periods.** How long police departments hold on to the potentially sensitive data about ordinary people’s lives that license scanners collect is a key civil liberties metric. Where police use ALPR we recommend a rule like New Hampshire’s, in which plate reads that don’t result in a watch list “hit” must be deleted within three minutes, or failing that, a retention period of no more than 48 hours. But the leading vendors all allow their customers to retain their ALPR data for as long as they like, with the exception of Flock, which[says](https://www.flocksafety.com/legal/flock-evidence-policy#:~:text=to-,one%20year) it imposes a one-year limit, and requires “approval from an elected official and/or a governing body” to retain data for more than the company’s 7-day default retention period. Otherwise, default retention periods amount to no more than suggestions. With a network as large as Flock’s (a[claimed](https://www.flocksafety.com/vs/axon) 20 billion monthly plate scans), a 7-day retention period (which the company[announced](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/despite-new-updates-flocks-creepy-cameras-remain-major-civil-liberties-threat) with great fanfare in an attempt to quiet opposition) still gives police departments far too much mass-surveillance power over people not suspected of wrongdoing. In the absence of vendor-imposed limits, customers may decide on very long retention periods; the NYPD, for example (which uses Motorola),[retains](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/public_information/post-final/license-plate-readers-lpr-nypd-impact-and-use-policy_4.9.21_final.pdf) its ALPR data for five years.
- **Federal sharing.** Flock says it doesn’t have any contracts with ICE or other federal agencies, though it has become clear that those agencies can access the company’s ALPR database through[proxies](https://www.404media.co/ice-taps-into-nationwide-ai-enabled-camera-network-data-shows/) in local departments. (In August 2025, Flock was[discovered](https://www.404media.co/cbp-had-access-to-more-than-80-000-flock-ai-cameras-nationwide/) to have been sharing data with CBP through an undisclosed pilot project, since[ended](https://apnews.com/article/immigration-abortion-license-plates-cameras-cc5f29df94a29ee2c6c2feb2151c8f5e) .) At the end of the day, once data about the lives of ordinary people in a community is collected, it’s very hard to control. Motorola, however, has a[contract](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/records-reveal-ice-using-mass-surveillance-database-track-people-aid-local-law)[with ICE](https://data.aclum.org/2025/10/07/flock-gives-law-enforcement-all-over-the-country-access-to-your-location/#:~:text=show%20ICE%20agents%20have%20direct%20access) ([through](https://www.aclunorcal.org/docs/DOCS_031319.pdf) Thompson-Reuters) permitting that agency to directly search Motorola’s surveillance database, so if your police department is contributing to that, you *know* your data is going to ICE, no intermediaries required.
- **Cloud and local storage and control.** In addition to all the questions raised by license plate surveillance, there are serious questions about private company access to that data, as we outlined in a recent[white paper](https://www.aclu.org/documents/surveillance-profits-and-the-police) . Local storage also offers more local control — if the data your local department collects is stored on its own computers and not accessible by the vendor, for example, then the vendor’s policy on sharing with ICE is no longer an issue. Local storage of data on police department’s own computers used to be common with ALPR systems, but today, with the trend toward cloud services, neither Flock nor Motorola allow their clients to store their data locally. Both claim to allow their customers “control” over their data, but that is a governance claim and not an infrastructure claim, and ultimately whoever holds the data truly controls it (unless it’s end-to-end encrypted). Axon does[offer](https://www.axon.com/help/release-notes/evidence-local/version-6-2.htm) a local storage solution, as do some other competitors, as discussed below.
- **AI imagery search.** Since its inception, basic license plate detection has collected license plate number data, snapshot stills of plates, and place/time data, but companies are now promising police departments new powers by pushing far beyond that. We recommend that communities require any ALPR vendors to stick to the basics. All the companies offer analysis of vehicle attributes, and some also offer more powerful free-form AI search of stored video or still imagery. Flock touts its ability to let officers search not just for license plates, but also for make, model, and other vehicle attributes and distinguishing characteristics, and to use free text AI searches to unleash modern video analytics not just for vehicle searches but also for people appearing in captured imagery. Motorola also collects other data about vehicles (but not people),[including](https://www.motorolasolutions.com/en_us/video-security-access-control/license-plate-recognition-camera-systems/vehiclemanager-lpr-analytics-software.html) “accessories, damage, and promotional writing or bumper stickers,” and[offers](https://www.motorolasolutions.com/content/dam/msi/docs/products/license-plate-recognition-systems/vigilant-vehiclemanager/vigilant_vehiclemanager_brochure.pdf) plain-language[AI search](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/machine-surveillance-is-being-super-charged-by-large-ai-models) of the imagery in its database. Axon offers structured[searches](https://www.axon.com/help/fleet-3/cameras-and-sensors/fleet/3/alpr/alpr-search-evidence.htm) for various vehicle attributes but doesn’t have the same level of wide-ranging AI search (except for within case files). It’s likely that whatever particular companies offer now, however, many or all will eventually offer such capabilities.
- **Suspicion generation.** Here Flock is definitely the worst,[touting](https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/tracking-alpr-cameras/surveillance-company-flock-now-using-ai-to-report-us-to-police-if-it-thinks-our-movement-patterns-are-suspicious) the ability to “detect patterns of suspicious activity across cities and states,” and generally opening up unprecedented new possibilities for fishing expeditions by allowing[in-depth AI searches](https://www.wired.com/story/flock-safety-os-investigate/) through data on people’s movements. Motorola also crosses that key line from investigative aids to[suspicion](https://www.motorolasolutions.com/en_us/video-security-access-control/license-plate-recognition-camera-systems/vehiclemanager-lpr-analytics-software.html)[generation](https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/tracking-alpr-cameras/surveillance-company-flock-now-using-ai-to-report-us-to-police-if-it-thinks-our-movement-patterns-are-suspicious) ; touting its ability to “reveal patterns, trends and associations which generate leads.” It doesn’t seem that its system aims to facilitate a true cold search for movement and association patterns to the extent of Flock. Axon doesn’t appear to offer suspicion generation capabilities at this time. But again, the various vendors’ AI offerings may change fast.
- **Use of NCIC database.** One key civil liberties protection around plate scanning is that the watch lists used by law enforcement be subject to checks and balances. Flock’s service runs plate scans against the FBI’s criminal database, the NCIC. It is murky exactly how this access works — the FBI refused to explain it to the author of an IPVM[research report](https://ipvm.com/reports/ncic-lpr) on the subject — but as we[have](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/how-to-fight-deployment-of-flock-and-other-mass-surveillance-license-plate-readers-in-your-community#:~:text=Database%20Use)[explained](https://www.aclu.org/wp-content/uploads/publications/flock_1.pdf#page=5) , it’s problematic for a number of reasons having to do with accuracy, due process, and timely updating of listings of which cars are flagged. In addition, one component of the NCIC is an “Immigration Violator” hotlist maintained by ICE, which can be a[backdoor way](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/are-your-local-police-using-flock-safety-alprs-scan-immigrants) of enabling local police to cooperate with the Trump Administration’s deportation drive. In addition to Flock,[Axon](https://www.axon.com/help/fleet-3/cameras-and-sensors/fleet/3/alpr/alpr-hotlists.htm) can also run their hits against this database. I wasn’t able to confirm whether Motorola also allows that functionality. At least[some](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2025-06/25_0606_st_lprmsr.pdf#page=35) of the smaller companies appear to[offer](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2025-06/25_0606_st_lprmsr.pdf#page=37)


Another potential check on the power of ALPR systems is use limitations. Flock has[in the past](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/flock-safety-credibility-lost-as-it-repeatedly-lies-to-city-councils-police-departments-and-public-across-the-country) promised to restrict “impermissible” searches, such as abortion-related searches in states like Illinois that ban the sharing of abortion data. More recently, the company[announced](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/despite-new-updates-flocks-creepy-cameras-remain-major-civil-liberties-threat) as part of its “updates” meant to mute criticism that it would let local departments decide what types of offenses other Flock customers can search their data for. The problem is that there is no effective enforcement mechanism behind these measures; they rely on an honor system in which police officers accurately and honestly describe the purpose of their search — something that[experience](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/police-audit-logs) has[shown](https://www.registerguard.com/story/news/local/2025/12/11/eugene-license-plate-camera-data-shared-outside-oregon/87704952007/) to be[ineffective](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/06/flock-safetys-feature-updates-cannot-make-automated-license-plate-readers-safe) .


### What matters most is not maximum capabilities but actual deployment contracts


As we have seen, there are significant differences among providers in how license plate scanning is done. But a community can often reach a contract with providers that restricts the capabilities that are deployed. For several[years](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/how-to-pump-the-brakes-on-your-police-departments-use-of-flocks-mass-surveillance-license-plate-readers) we have[urged](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/tracking-alpr-cameras/how-to-fight-deployment-of-flock-and-other-mass-surveillance-license-plate-readers-in-your-community) cities to do this. Just because Flock and Motorola do nationwide sharing and AI search doesn’t mean that a police department needs to use (or a city council needs to allow its police department to use) such capabilities. Defaults are important, but for a jurisdiction that is determined to deploy ALPR, the most important differences among companies that community members should look at are what those vendors will allow localities to control.


Community members attuned to privacy and civil liberties should also push city councils — or state legislatures — to put limits into law through general ordinances that remain in effect even as contracts and vendors come and go over the years. The differences among vendors in how they provide ALPR services are governed by corporate strategy rather than law, which means they can be changed in an instant by the companies. Communities should not gain too much comfort from what companies are and are not doing right now, but instead keep their eye on the longer game by putting protections into law.


When Denver decided to[discontinue](https://www.9news.com/article/news/local/denver-removing-flock-cameras-new-axon-contract/73-640b5af3-7c87-4fea-8aa1-2510ad3257b8) its contract with Flock earlier this year, it ([hastily and unwisely](https://www.aclu-co.org/press-releases/community-organizations-and-denver-surveillance-task-force-members-ask-denver-city-councilors-to-vote-no-on-axon-alpr-contract/) ) switched to a new vendor (Axon). But what mattered more than the change in vendor was the change in how ALPR was operated; the new contract shortened the data retention period (from 30 days to a still-too-long 21 days), restricted data sharing, and banned federal access to Denverites’ data. Denver probably could have obtained those same terms with any vendor.


Overall, the default behavior of a company’s ALPR offerings becomes less important, and the control it gives customers becomes more important.


- **Choosing a short retention period.** Motorola and Axon allow a customer to retain data for as long as they want, and despite its new suggestion of 7 days, down from 30, Flock only hard-caps retention at a year. But customers of all three companies (and, my sense is, their smaller competitors’) can still set very short data retention limits as we recommend.
- **Disallow nationwide sharing.** Flock and Motorola, which both offer nationwide data sharing, both allow customers to not participate (but often cajole them into participating, because it is in the companies’ financial interest for them to do so). Note, however, that vendors also can allow regional, statewide, or department-by-department sharing, so access to your community’s data can be fairly broad even without nationwide sharing. Axon doesn’t offer nationwide sharing but does have built-in functionality for case-by-case sharing among departments. The more broadly data is shared, the more points there are for ICE, CBP, or anyone else to access it through a cooperative department or officer.
- **Choosing local data storage.** On the other hand, when it comes to local data storage, a Flock or Motorola customer doesn’t have the option to not use their cloud services so far as we can tell, whereas customers of Axon, Rekor, and other vendors do.
- **Decline AI analytics.** It appears that police department customers can’t opt out of basic vehicle attribution recognition capabilities offered by all the biggest companies. The freeform AI searches of still and video data that Flock offers[appear](https://www.flocksafety.com/products/flock-freeform) to be a separate product that a customer could simply decline to pay for. It’s less clear whether customers can opt out with Motorola, but the company may be willing to agree to disable that functionality to make a sale.
- **Decline suspicion-generating AI.** As far as we can tell, use of Flock and Motorola’s AI algorithmic suspicion-generation is not required, so in theory a municipality could insist through an ordinance and in vendor contracts that such a capability not be made available to a client police department.


###


### The bottom line


Overall, a comparative look at the ALPR marketplace through a civil liberties lens yields several takeaways:


- If a jurisdiction decides to allow license scanners to be installed, how that system operates is more important than which vendor provides it, though considerations about the overall ethics of a company are certainly worth taking into account.
- When looking at vendors, the most important question is whether they provide the *option* to impose restrictions that protect privacy and civil liberties.
- If a community doesn’t impose strong conditions such as data retention limits, switching from Flock to another ALPR provider could leave residents’ civil liberties in equally bad or even worse shape.
- Communities should address ALPR policies democratically and they should impose them through legal limits on license scanning rather than through internal police department policies or vendor contracts that will be repeatedly re-negotiated as years pass.


Again, the most civil liberties protective step that a municipality can take is to spurn license plate scanners altogether. But where that’s not possible, community members should not think that simply abandoning Flock for another vendor will necessarily make things better.

### As Public Opposition to Flock Grows, ACLU Responds to Surveillance Company’s “New” Updates


NEW YORK – Amid nationwide outcry against its automatic license plate readers, Flock Safety announced today that it will reduce its standard data retention policy and allegedly provide more control over local data searches, among other changes. However, according to American Civil Liberties Union’s new analysis, many of the proposed changes seem to be a thinly veiled PR attempt to counter communities’ genuine privacy concerns with its mass surveillance system with largely hollow security promises, rather than an earnest effort to address them. While the ACLU acknowledges one potentially positive development, most of the proposed changes stand little chance of making a positive difference for civil liberties. “Transforming an exceptionally dangerous mass surveillance system into one that is fully protective of civil rights and civil liberties is a difficult, if not impossible task. That is even more the case with a company like Flock, whose nearly $1 billion in venture capitalist funding has locked it into an operational model that seeks to trade our privacy for massive profits,” said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at ACLU. “Given that Flock’s latest announcement still appears more focused on addressing a PR problem than the significant privacy and other harms its products create, we will continue to analyze the company’s proposals fairly and honestly. We just won’t be holding our breath.” Flock operates more than 120,000 automatic license plate readers in at least 6,000 cities across the country, raising serious concerns around mass surveillance, data privacy, and how police and the government can use this data to go after immigrants, protestors, and others. Just this week, the Institute for Justice published a database with more than 100 incidents of ALPR abuse, including romantic stalking, wrongful stops and detentions, non-law enforcement use, and other types of misconduct. One of the changes announced is that Flock will decrease its standard data retention option to one week from 30 days. This seems positive at first blush, but as the ACLU’s breakdown explains, the devil will be in the details. For example, an exception to the data retention policy is something called “Evidence Mode, which is “when a search is tied to a case number, that data is preserved instead of aging out after 7 days.” As the ACLU notes, “If ‘Evidence Mode’ only retains hit result data that police determine may be evidence in an active investigation of a specific case, then the change may be a positive one. But if Evidence Mode triggers the retention of any ALPR data that is searched, then the new mode could indefinitely retain all the ALPR data Flock collects and shares nationally.” Another “change” the company is implementing is that local police will be able to decide what types of offenses other Flock customers can search their data for. The ACLU contends that this is not new. Flock has attempted this before, and the security measure failed because police were easily able to circumvent the system’s requirement that they input the purpose of their search. Finally, Flock announced that in response to the reports of police abuse, they will now require reasons for a search, and that they plan to universally roll out its audit assistance tool to detect police misuse. Flock’s announcement fails to note how easily users have circumvented “search reason” security measures in the past or how its new policy improves the quality of the feature. And while providing “Audit Assistance” to all departments makes sense, the ACLU notes that there is no evidence that the tool works consistently to address what the Washington Post observed is a growing pattern of police officers turning Flock into a personal stalking tool. To determine the efficacy of this tool, Flock needs to have it analyzed by an independent evaluator. Until then, the ACLU says, “we don’t know if the tool is a real security measure or just window dressing.” Dozens of communities across the country have successfully convinced their leaders to cancel Flock contracts, suspend their ALPR programs, or deactivate the cameras, with many more cities considering new legislation to rein in this mass warrantless surveillance tech. In June, the ACLU launched its “Get the Flock Out” campaign to bring together the litigation, advocacy, and legislative efforts of ACLU affiliates in each state, show how communities across the country are fighting back against the spread of Flock and other license plate readers, and lay out how lawmakers at the local, state, and federal level can best protect our rights.
